opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on how narrowly you define the use case, and that's actually where open source has its best shot.

If you're asking whether an open model, out of the box, will beat the best proprietary model at everything, generally the answer has been no, or at least not consistently. The frontier labs have enormous compute budgets, a lot of proprietary data, and a lot of post-training expertise. But that's rarely the right question for an application builder. Most real applications don't need a model that can write sonnets, solve olympiad math, and debug Kubernetes all at once. They need something that does one or a handful of things very reliably, at a cost and latency that make the product viable.

So the way I'd assess it is pretty empirical. First, define what "better" means for you, and it's usually not just accuracy. It's accuracy on your distribution of inputs, plus cost per query, latency, and things like whether you can run it on your own infrastructure for privacy or compliance reasons. Second, build an evaluation set that reflects your actual workload, not a public benchmark, because public benchmarks get saturated and gamed, and they often don't correlate with what your users care about. That's one reason we did Chatbot Arena: to get human preference signals from real usage rather than relying only on static tests.

Then you compare. And what we've seen again and again is that once you take a strong open model and fine-tune it on domain-specific data, or put it inside a well-designed system with retrieval, tool use, and maybe several model calls checking each other, it can match or exceed a general-purpose proprietary model on that specific task, often at a fraction of the cost. Vicuna was an early example: a fairly small fine-tune that got surprisingly close to ChatGPT on conversational quality, which told us that a lot of the gap was post-training data and not just scale.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that the gap between open and closed has been shrinking over time, and the pace at which open models catch up has been accelerating. So even if today the proprietary model wins on your eval, you should design your system so you can swap models easily. Treat the model as a component. That's a systems lesson we've learned many times: whoever controls the abstraction layer has flexibility, and flexibility matters a lot when the underlying technology is changing this fast.

r001.rationale: It describes combining retrieval, tool use, and multiple model calls in a system, which communicates an application composed of multiple components.

r002.rationale: It says a strong open model fine-tuned on domain-specific data can match or exceed a general-purpose proprietary model on that specific task.

r003.rationale: It discusses domain-specific data and retrieval, but does not state that understanding the structure of an application's data improves accuracy.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that you can't really assess it in the abstract. "Better" only means something relative to a particular task and a particular set of users. That's actually one of the reasons we started Chatbot Arena at Berkeley. The existing benchmarks were static, they were getting contaminated, and they didn't reflect what people actually wanted to do with these models. So we said, let's just let real people ask real questions, show them two anonymous answers side by side, and have them vote. Then you aggregate millions of those pairwise comparisons into an Elo-style rating.

What you see when you do that is interesting. On the overall leaderboard, the frontier proprietary models have generally stayed ahead, but the gap has been closing steadily. And when you slice by category, the picture gets much more nuanced. For coding, for math, for certain languages, open models like the Llama family, DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, can be very competitive and sometimes come out on top in specific segments.

But the real question for an application is a different one. If you're building something for a specific domain, say customer support for your product, or extracting information from legal contracts, you have data the general model has never seen. You can fine-tune an open model on that data, you can build retrieval around it, you can run it on your own infrastructure for a fraction of the cost and with your data staying in-house. For that narrow task, the fine-tuned open model can absolutely beat a general-purpose proprietary model. We've seen this again and again.

So my approach is: don't trust the aggregate leaderboard for your decision. Build an evaluation that mirrors your actual workload, ideally with the same kind of blind pairwise comparison, and measure. Cost and latency go into that equation too, because a model that's five percent worse but ten times cheaper changes what you can afford to build. And the fact that open models let you own and iterate on the whole stack, that's a structural advantage that compounds over time. That's the same argument I'd make for Spark or Ray in the systems world. Openness wins when the problem is specialized and the users have their own data.

r001.rationale: It describes combining an open model with retrieval built around it as part of a specialized application.

r002.rationale: It says application-specific data unseen by a general model can be used to fine-tune an open model that beats the general-purpose model on a narrow task.

r003.rationale: It discusses using domain data, fine-tuning, and retrieval, but does not say that knowing the data’s structure improves accuracy.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to be specific about what you mean by outperform. Are you measuring accuracy on a particular task, latency, cost, or some combination of these? You don’t necessarily need a model that is better at everything. You need an application that is better at what your users care about.

An open-source model gives you the opportunity to customize it, bring in your own data, and optimize the system around that use case. So a smaller model, with the right data and the right surrounding tools, can potentially outperform a much larger general-purpose model on a narrow task.

The way to assess that is to build an evaluation that reflects the actual workload. Compare the complete applications on representative inputs, look at where they fail, and measure the cost and latency at the quality level you need. It’s an empirical question. Being open source doesn’t automatically make something better, but it gives you more control over how you get there.

r001.rationale: It describes a smaller model combined with use-case data and surrounding tools, and says to evaluate the complete application—communicating an application made from multiple components.

r002.rationale: It says access to your own data can help a smaller model potentially outperform a much larger general-purpose model on a narrow task; in context, that addresses ChatGPT for a specific use case.

r003.rationale: It says to bring in use-case data but does not state that knowing the data’s structure improves accuracy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between the model and the application. You may not need a model that is better than ChatGPT at everything. You need a system that is better at the particular task your users care about.

For a narrow use case, an open-source model can be adapted to your data, connected to the right information, and integrated with your workflow. That can give you a very competitive application, even if the underlying model is less capable in general.

The way to assess that is to evaluate on representative tasks using your own data. Look at the quality of the answers, but also the cost, latency, and requirements around privacy and control. It's an empirical question. For some applications, a proprietary model will be the best choice. For others, a smaller, specialized open-source model may give you a better overall result.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes the model from the application and mentions data, information, and workflow, but it does not clearly describe the application as a composition of multiple components.

r002.rationale: It says a system tailored to a particular task can be better at that task than ChatGPT, and that adapting an open-source model to your data and connecting it to relevant information can produce a competitive application.

r003.rationale: It says to adapt the model to your data, but does not state that understanding the data’s structure improves accuracy.
